Digital Voices

By: Laura Byrne | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Technology is bridging the gap for those without a voice, but plenty to say.

Unique Selling Point:
Augmentative and Alternative Communication devices have existed for as long as there have been people who need help in expressing what those of us take for granted every day.From something as simple as a piece of paper and a pen or a colour-coded board, to cutting edge programming and electronics, the range is endless. But increasingly, tablets, eye gaze technology and voice synthesis is helping those without a voice to speak for themselves, in their own unique way...and without having to sound like Stephen Hawking or Google Maps.

Summary:
Voice loss can be caused by innumerable factors: stroke, motor vehicle accident, motor neurone disease (MND), cancer... Many children born with cerebral palsy never develop spoken language. Lacking an intelligible voice does not mean you have nothing to say, but the voiceless are amongst society's most vulnerable, unable to express likes and dislikes, to refuse consent, or to report the abuse and neglect that so many face. Even for those lucky enough to have access to AAC devices, the voices available are robotic, unemotional, impersonal...lacking all of the elements of age, gender, and character with which we broadcast our identities.
It was this problem that Rupal Patel decided to tackle after witnessing two AAC users, one a middle-aged man and one a young girl, speaking to each other with exactly the same synthesised adult male voice. She decided that even those who have never developed language should be able to speak with their own voices, and VocaliD was born. VocaliD synthesises voices for text-to-speech devices using the sounds vocalised by the disabled AAC user, filtered through the voice of a donor of similar age and background, to create a voice that is appropriate and unique to each user.
VocaliD is the only company providing this service, but there are people everywhere working to help the voiceless speak. At Chris Hani Baragwaneth Hospital, the MND clinic offers message banking for those who will lose their voices to the disease. At New Hope School, Pretoria, one learner is making use of a text-to-speech device that speaks Afrikaans, part of a CSIR project to provide AAC in all 11 South African languages.
We will take a look into the wide world of AAC, and shed light on some of the spectacular ways in which technology can help those without a voice participate in a society in which vocal expression is so central.

Further information:
There are various types of AAC devices. These are classed as either low-tech (eg a colour coded board on which a user, assisted by a partner, can scan through symbols or letters to string together messages) or high-tech (tablets, voice or switch-activated electronic devices and of course eye gaze devices, which use infrared to track the user's eye movement, allowing those who are severely physically impaired to 'move' a mouse over a screen, type, or select from a range of symbols). Electronic devices can be as simple as a recorder/speaker than allows for one or two messages to be stored and played back with the push of a button - or text-to-speech programmes that will vocalise predictive text or typed words to generate novel information based on the user's desires.
Voice and message banking are services offered to those who know they will lose their voices, but have enough vocal ability left to store that voice. Message banking is simpler: the user records numerous 'messages' (words and phrases) they anticipate needing, from the sound of a laugh, to calling a dog, to 'I love you' to daily requirements like food and hygiene. An extension of message banking is legacy banking, in which the user stores a particular story or message intended for a particular person - for example, a message to play her daughter on her wedding day. This is the service Bara offers.
Voice banking is more sophisticated: the user records their own voice reading a set series of phrases that capture all the phonemes of the language. These are then used by a text-to-speech device to synthesis an electronic version of the user's own voice that sounds more or less like them. So far, this is not widely available in South Africa, and there are no local companies offering it.
VocaliD is therefore a step above the rest, offering people who have never been able to speak the chance to have a synthesised voice that is unique to them, and contains something of their own vocalisation. Other companies exist that will create unique voices that are age-appropriate and might be generated from a donor's voice (a sibling for example).
We will speak to Rupal Patel via Skype, and then bring the story home with various case studies and experts in South Africa. VocaliD does not have any South African users but they do have about 5 'voice bankers' so we will speak to one of them.
We will visit the Bara clinic to watch a message banking session, interview a therapist and watch the clinic at work. We will then visit one of the MND/message banking patients at home to see how they use their recorded voice.
We will interview a scientist at CSIR regarding the development of indigenous language AAC software. We will then visit New Hope School to speak to Alexander, a Grade 1 learner who makes use of the Afrikaans text-to-speech programme.
We will speak to Kevin Jordan, an MND sufferer who uses eye gaze technology to communicate and to control the appliances in his house.
Time permitting, we will interview someone from Inclusive Solutions, the company that imports the majority of AAC devices into South Africa. Desirae can demonstrate to us how the devices work, allow our presenter to try them out, and talk about some of the challenges that families face when they start using AAC.

Press Release:


The ability to speak is something many of us take for granted, but for those who have had strokes, accidents, throat cancer or been diagnosed with Motor neuron disease, voice loss can be a devastating reality. Robotic machines such as the one used by Stephen Hawking have helped the voiceless communicate, but they sound impersonal and generic. Now researchers are creating unique, personalised voices for those who can’t speak for themselves.

Script:


UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Can your machine tell me what your name is?
Nasi Sibaya: N – A – S – I. Nacey.
VO1: Nasi Sibaya is nine years old. He has severe cerebral palsy, which produces uncontrollable muscular movements, and prevents him from forming words.
UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: This device works in English – is it difficult for you to communicate in English?
Nasi Sibaya: Easy.
Claire Mawisa: It’s easy? Do you speak English at home?
Nasi Sibaya: I speak Zulu at home.
VO2: Nasi’s eye gaze device tracks the movement of his eyes over a screen, then converts the message into synthesised speech – with the voice of an adult British man.
LINK 1: My voice is my identity. It tells you who I am. Every time you use your voice, you send a million tiny signals about your gender, age, background, even your mood. Now imagine losing all of that.
UPSOUND: Desirae Pillay: AAC is an acronym for augmentative and alternative communication. Augmentative to add to your current speech, so if you have some words, some signs, then we add a system to help you. If you are using an alternative system it means you have no other way of communicating.
VO3: Desirae Pillay is technology advisor at Inclusive Solutions, a company that supplies AAC to South African users.
UPSOUND: Desirae Pillay: I know people who due to their disability, they stay at home 98% of the time. But it’s important to say things like change the tv channel or that was really funny.
VO4: In other words, just because you can’t speak doesn’t mean you have nothing to say. At worst, the voiceless are vulnerable to abuse; at best, they are often cut off from the world around them.
UPSOUND: Desirae Pillay: When we look at giving a voice to a child that has never had one, we are giving them an opportunity to take part in conversations, to tell jokes, to tell stories, that they’ve never had the opportunity to do before.
VO5: But voice loss is also acquired, through injury, stroke, or disease.
UPSOUND: Kevin Jordan: My biggest fear was not to be able to talk. Because if you can’t talk, you’re in effect in prison in your own body.
VO6: Kevin Jordan has motor neurone disease, a progressive, incurable wasting of nerves and muscles – including the ones that produce your voice. He can still speak, but uses an eye gaze device to communicate online, and to run his charity, You and Me Versus MND.
UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Do you feel well represented by the computerised voice?
Kevin Jordan: I actually find it quite entertaining changing the voices. I’d rather be able to talk in any voice than no voice at all.
UPSOUND: Stephen Hawking: I identify with this voice and have no intention of changing it for a more naturally sounding one.
VO7: We’re all familiar with Stephen Hawking’s robotic tones – they became part of his persona. But when five children in the same classroom speak with the same adult AAC voice, their individual identities can go unheard.
UPSOUND Rupal Patel: if you have a prosthesis, whether it’s a leg or it’s an arm or it’s a voice, people should have choices so that they can find the one that fits right.
VO8: Speech language clinician Rupal Patel founded Boston-based company VocaliD, after witnessing a grown man and a young girl conversing using identical adult male AAC voices.
UPSOUND: Rupal Patel: And I thought, well if they have the ability to still make sound that’s unique to them, why can we not harness that sound to create digital voices that are unique to them.
VO9: VocaliD uses the limited vocalisation that someone like Nasi can produce, and combines it with donated voices.
UPSOUND: Rupal Patel: When we make a customised voice for someone, we take a little bit of their voice and we blend it together with those surrogate talkers to create a unique voice that fits them in age and gender and accent and even preferences.
VO10: VocaliD’s crowdsourced voice bank features 26 000 donors from as young as 6 to as old as 91, in 120 countries. Over 140 people speak with a custom-made VocaliD voice.
UPSOUND: Rupal Patel: You see people who are taking huge communication risks that they weren’t before. They’re now talking to strangers, they’re now going into public spaces where they’re wanting to use their voice. They’re feeling ownership of their voice.
VO11: VocaliD and other companies also offer the opportunity to bank your voice before you lose it, so that your AAC device can speak with a synthesised version of you. In South Africa, voice banking is rare, due partly to cost. But a team at Chris Hani Baragwaneth Hospital is offering patients another way to preserve their vocal identities.
UPSOUND: John Nzima: To use a voice device it’s not to say my brain it’s not working. I’m also a person, and a human being like anyone.
VO12: Like Kevin, John Nzima suffers from a progressive neurological condition. While he can still speak, he is banking the words and messages he will need when the disease claims his voice.
UPSOUND: Hayley Hochfelden: What we aim to do with message banking is to record that person’s voice, the way it sounds, the way they would answer a question or tell a joke. And then we transfer those messages onto a device and the patient will then use the device to communicate later on in their disease.
VO13: Speech therapist Hayley Hochfelden coordinates the message banking programme specifically for those facing inevitable voice loss.
UPSOUND: Hayley Hochfelden: If you are unable to communicate you are often left out of some of the major decisions that will be made around your end of life care. So it’s very important that we ensure that they have access to communication to ensure that they not only have quality of life while they’re with us but they also have quality of dying when they get to the very terminal phases of the disease.
LINK 2: ‘I’m hungry’ – ‘I’m in pain’ – ‘I love you’ – Imagine you are about to lose your voice forever. Could you choose 50 phrases to serve all your needs for the rest of your life?
UPSOUND: Hayley Hochfelden: It’s an incredible thing to have to actualise and to record out loud the fact that you won’t be able to do basic things in the future.
VO14: Early diagnosis is vital so patients can bank their messages before their voices become slurred. The banking process itself is emotional and taxing. But the impact is enormous.
UPSOUND: Hayley Hochfelden: It’s like watching someone being able to breathe again. Losing your ability to communicate is suffocating. It’s being trapped inside your body, not being able to control what happens to you, where you go, what meals you get. As simple as what clothes you put on in the morning.
UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Does it make you feel better that you have the opportunity to bank your voice?
John Nzima: Yes, it makes me stronger because I know that I can communicate, I can speak with the people
Claire Mawisa: Did you feel like your recorded messages represented you well? Like yes, that’s me.
John Nzima: I feel like myself. I feel like myself.
VO15: It’s possible to bank messages in any language, but the content is limited. A synthesised voice can generate novel content but…
LINK 3: [AAC] Molweni ninjani, nisaphila. [Claire] As you can see it’s all well and good if you speak English, but what if you prefer to communicate in one of South Africa’s other languages?
UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Hoe het jy gevoel toe jy dit vir die eerste keer gebruik het en Afrikaans kon praat?
Alexander Avenant: Ek was baie opgewonde.
Stephanie: Was iets vir jou snaaks gewees?
Alexander: Die oom stem het my baie laat lag.
VO16: Alexander Avenant cannot speak due to brain damage he sustained as a baby. Although his foster family is Afrikaans-speaking, he had to use English-language AAC – until now.
UPSOUND: Karen Calteaux: Our languages are what they call under-resourced languages, so there’s not a lot of resources or data available for our languages.
VO17: Dr Karen Calteaux and her speech technology team at the CSIR Meraka Institute designed Qfrency: synthesised voices for all 11 official South African languages.
UPSOUND: Karen Calteaux: The African languages are tonal languages, modelling tone or getting a computer to reproduce tone is very very difficult. So that is ongoing research for us.
UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Dink jy wanner jou maatjies die stem hoor, hoor hulle jou?
Alexander Avenant: Nee, hulle hoor die oom se stem.
VO18: AAC remains a far from perfect communication tool. And while the technology is constantly evolving, there’s a lot we can do to improve our treatment of the voiceless.
UPSOUND Kevin Jordan [AAC]: Unable to speak is a disability which is rarely thought of. Voiceless people are still people, with opinions, thoughts, views and feelings. Surely, they deserve to be heard.
UPSOUND Claire Mawisa: What’s the future for AAC?
Desirae Pillay: I hope to see more people using it earlier. I hope that it won’t have the stigma that it has. I would love to see every child from a very young age given their voice.

PROMO1 – 10 SECONDS
VO: The causes of voice loss range from injury to disease to cerebral palsy. How is technology helping the voiceless speak for themselves?

PROMO2 – 15 SECONDS
VO: Your voice broadcasts your age, gender, identity and even mood. Imagine losing it forever.
UPSOUND: Kevin Jordan: I’d rather be able to talk in any voice than no voice at all.

PROMO3 – 15 SECONDS
UPSOUND: Stephen Hawking: I identify with this voice.
VO: We’re all familiar with Stephen Hawking’s robotic tones, but imagine you had to speak with the voice of a machine.
UPSOUND: Kevin Jordan: Voiceless people are still people, with opinions, thoughts, views and feelings.

PROMO4 – 30 SECONDS
UPSOUND: Claire: Hoe het jy gevoel toe jy dit die eerste keer gebruik het en Afrikaans kon praat?
Alexander: Ek was baie opgewonde.
VO: Alexander Avenant can’t speak due to brain damage he sustained as a baby. But that doesn’t mean he has nothing to say. Technology is helping people like him find a voice.
UPSOUND: Hayley Hochfelden: It’s like watching someone being able to breathe again. Losing your ability to communicate is suffocating.

Nasi Sibaya: N – A – S – I. Nacey. VO1: Nasi Sibaya is nine years old. He has severe cerebral palsy, which produces uncontrollable muscular movements, and prevents him from forming words. UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: This device works in English – is it difficult for you to communicate in English? Nasi Sibaya: Easy. Claire Mawisa: It’s easy? Do you speak English at home? Nasi Sibaya: I speak Zulu at home. VO2: Nasi’s eye gaze device tracks the movement of his eyes over a screen, then converts the message into synthesised speech – with the voice of an adult British man. LINK 1: My voice is my identity. It tells you who I am. Every time you use your voice, you send a million tiny signals about your gender, age, background, even your mood. Now imagine losing all of that. UPSOUND: Desirae Pillay: AAC is an acronym for augmentative and alternative communication. Augmentative to add to your current speech, so if you have some words, some signs, then we add a system to help you. If you are using an alternative system it means you have no other way of communicating. VO3: Desirae Pillay is technology advisor at Inclusive Solutions, a company that supplies AAC to South African users. UPSOUND: Desirae Pillay: I know people who due to their disability, they stay at home 98% of the time. But it’s important to say things like change the tv channel or that was really funny. VO4: In other words, just because you can’t speak doesn’t mean you have nothing to say. At worst, the voiceless are vulnerable to abuse; at best, they are often cut off from the world around them. UPSOUND: Desirae Pillay: When we look at giving a voice to a child that has never had one, we are giving them an opportunity to take part in conversations, to tell jokes, to tell stories, that they’ve never had the opportunity to do before. VO5: But voice loss is also acquired, through injury, stroke, or disease. UPSOUND: Kevin Jordan: My biggest fear was not to be able to talk. Because if you can’t talk, you’re in effect in prison in your own body. VO6: Kevin Jordan has motor neurone disease, a progressive, incurable wasting of nerves and muscles – including the ones that produce your voice. He can still speak, but uses an eye gaze device to communicate online, and to run his charity, You and Me Versus MND. UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Do you feel well represented by the computerised voice? Kevin Jordan: I actually find it quite entertaining changing the voices. I’d rather be able to talk in any voice than no voice at all. UPSOUND: Stephen Hawking: I identify with this voice and have no intention of changing it for a more naturally sounding one. VO7: We’re all familiar with Stephen Hawking’s robotic tones – they became part of his persona. But when five children in the same classroom speak with the same adult AAC voice, their individual identities can go unheard. UPSOUND Rupal Patel: if you have a prosthesis, whether it’s a leg or it’s an arm or it’s a voice, people should have choices so that they can find the one that fits right. VO8: Speech language clinician Rupal Patel founded Boston-based company VocaliD, after witnessing a grown man and a young girl conversing using identical adult male AAC voices. UPSOUND: Rupal Patel: And I thought, well if they have the ability to still make sound that’s unique to them, why can we not harness that sound to create digital voices that are unique to them. VO9: VocaliD uses the limited vocalisation that someone like Nasi can produce, and combines it with donated voices. UPSOUND: Rupal Patel: When we make a customised voice for someone, we take a little bit of their voice and we blend it together with those surrogate talkers to create a unique voice that fits them in age and gender and accent and even preferences. VO10: VocaliD’s crowdsourced voice bank features 26 000 donors from as young as 6 to as old as 91, in 120 countries. Over 140 people speak with a custom-made VocaliD voice. UPSOUND: Rupal Patel: You see people who are taking huge communication risks that they weren’t before. They’re now talking to strangers, they’re now going into public spaces where they’re wanting to use their voice. They’re feeling ownership of their voice. VO11: VocaliD and other companies also offer the opportunity to bank your voice before you lose it, so that your AAC device can speak with a synthesised version of you. In South Africa, voice banking is rare, due partly to cost. But a team at Chris Hani Baragwaneth Hospital is offering patients another way to preserve their vocal identities. UPSOUND: John Nzima: To use a voice device it’s not to say my brain it’s not working. I’m also a person, and a human being like anyone. VO12: Like Kevin, John Nzima suffers from a progressive neurological condition. While he can still speak, he is banking the words and messages he will need when the disease claims his voice. UPSOUND: Hayley Hochfelden: What we aim to do with message banking is to record that person’s voice, the way it sounds, the way they would answer a question or tell a joke. And then we transfer those messages onto a device and the patient will then use the device to communicate later on in their disease. VO13: Speech therapist Hayley Hochfelden coordinates the message banking programme specifically for those facing inevitable voice loss. UPSOUND: Hayley Hochfelden: If you are unable to communicate you are often left out of some of the major decisions that will be made around your end of life care. So it’s very important that we ensure that they have access to communication to ensure that they not only have quality of life while they’re with us but they also have quality of dying when they get to the very terminal phases of the disease. LINK 2: ‘I’m hungry’ – ‘I’m in pain’ – ‘I love you’ – Imagine you are about to lose your voice forever. Could you choose 50 phrases to serve all your needs for the rest of your life? UPSOUND: Hayley Hochfelden: It’s an incredible thing to have to actualise and to record out loud the fact that you won’t be able to do basic things in the future. VO14: Early diagnosis is vital so patients can bank their messages before their voices become slurred. The banking process itself is emotional and taxing. But the impact is enormous. UPSOUND: Hayley Hochfelden: It’s like watching someone being able to breathe again. Losing your ability to communicate is suffocating. It’s being trapped inside your body, not being able to control what happens to you, where you go, what meals you get. As simple as what clothes you put on in the morning. UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Does it make you feel better that you have the opportunity to bank your voice? John Nzima: Yes, it makes me stronger because I know that I can communicate, I can speak with the people Claire Mawisa: Did you feel like your recorded messages represented you well? Like yes, that’s me. John Nzima: I feel like myself. I feel like myself. VO15: It’s possible to bank messages in any language, but the content is limited. A synthesised voice can generate novel content but… LINK 3: [AAC] Molweni ninjani, nisaphila. [Claire] As you can see it’s all well and good if you speak English, but what if you prefer to communicate in one of South Africa’s other languages? UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Hoe het jy gevoel toe jy dit vir die eerste keer gebruik het en Afrikaans kon praat? Alexander Avenant: Ek was baie opgewonde. Stephanie: Was iets vir jou snaaks gewees? Alexander: Die oom stem het my baie laat lag. VO16: Alexander Avenant cannot speak due to brain damage he sustained as a baby. Although his foster family is Afrikaans-speaking, he had to use English-language AAC – until now. UPSOUND: Karen Calteaux: Our languages are what they call under-resourced languages, so there’s not a lot of resources or data available for our languages. VO17: Dr Karen Calteaux and her speech technology team at the CSIR Meraka Institute designed Qfrency: synthesised voices for all 11 official South African languages. UPSOUND: Karen Calteaux: The African languages are tonal languages, modelling tone or getting a computer to reproduce tone is very very difficult. So that is ongoing research for us. UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Dink jy wanner jou maatjies die stem hoor, hoor hulle jou? Alexander Avenant: Nee, hulle hoor die oom se stem. VO18: AAC remains a far from perfect communication tool. And while the technology is constantly evolving, there’s a lot we can do to improve our treatment of the voiceless. UPSOUND Kevin Jordan [AAC]: Unable to speak is a disability which is rarely thought of. Voiceless people are still people, with opinions, thoughts, views and feelings. Surely, they deserve to be heard. UPSOUND Claire Mawisa: What’s the future for AAC? Desirae Pillay: I hope to see more people using it earlier. I hope that it won’t have the stigma that it has. I would love to see every child from a very young age given their voice. PROMO1 – 10 SECONDS VO: The causes of voice loss range from injury to disease to cerebral palsy. How is technology helping the voiceless speak for themselves? PROMO2 – 15 SECONDS VO: Your voice broadcasts your age, gender, identity and even mood. Imagine losing it forever. UPSOUND: Kevin Jordan: I’d rather be able to talk in any voice than no voice at all. PROMO3 – 15 SECONDS UPSOUND: Stephen Hawking: I identify with this voice. VO: We’re all familiar with Stephen Hawking’s robotic tones, but imagine you had to speak with the voice of a machine. UPSOUND: Kevin Jordan: Voiceless people are still people, with opinions, thoughts, views and feelings. PROMO4 – 30 SECONDS UPSOUND: Claire: Hoe het jy gevoel toe jy dit die eerste keer gebruik het en Afrikaans kon praat? Alexander: Ek was baie opgewonde. VO: Alexander Avenant can’t speak due to brain damage he sustained as a baby. But that doesn’t mean he has nothing to say. Technology is helping people like him find a voice. UPSOUND: Hayley Hochfelden: It’s like watching someone being able to breathe again. Losing your ability to communicate is suffocating.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Technology is bridging the gap for those without a voice, but plenty to say.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Augmentative and Alternative Communication devices have existed for as long as there have been people who need help in expressing what those of us take for granted every day.From something as simple as a piece of paper and a pen or a colour-coded board, to cutting edge programming and electronics, the range is endless. But increasingly, tablets, eye gaze technology and voice synthesis is helping those without a voice to speak for themselves, in their own unique way...and without having to sound like Stephen Hawking or Google Maps.
metadata.Summary: Voice loss can be caused by innumerable factors: stroke, motor vehicle accident, motor neurone disease (MND), cancer... Many children born with cerebral palsy never develop spoken language. Lacking an intelligible voice does not mean you have nothing to say, but the voiceless are amongst society's most vulnerable, unable to express likes and dislikes, to refuse consent, or to report the abuse and neglect that so many face. Even for those lucky enough to have access to AAC devices, the voices available are robotic, unemotional, impersonal...lacking all of the elements of age, gender, and character with which we broadcast our identities. It was this problem that Rupal Patel decided to tackle after witnessing two AAC users, one a middle-aged man and one a young girl, speaking to each other with exactly the same synthesised adult male voice. She decided that even those who have never developed language should be able to speak with their own voices, and VocaliD was born. VocaliD synthesises voices for text-to-speech devices using the sounds vocalised by the disabled AAC user, filtered through the voice of a donor of similar age and background, to create a voice that is appropriate and unique to each user. VocaliD is the only company providing this service, but there are people everywhere working to help the voiceless speak. At Chris Hani Baragwaneth Hospital, the MND clinic offers message banking for those who will lose their voices to the disease. At New Hope School, Pretoria, one learner is making use of a text-to-speech device that speaks Afrikaans, part of a CSIR project to provide AAC in all 11 South African languages. We will take a look into the wide world of AAC, and shed light on some of the spectacular ways in which technology can help those without a voice participate in a society in which vocal expression is so central.
metadata.Further information: There are various types of AAC devices. These are classed as either low-tech (eg a colour coded board on which a user, assisted by a partner, can scan through symbols or letters to string together messages) or high-tech (tablets, voice or switch-activated electronic devices and of course eye gaze devices, which use infrared to track the user's eye movement, allowing those who are severely physically impaired to 'move' a mouse over a screen, type, or select from a range of symbols). Electronic devices can be as simple as a recorder/speaker than allows for one or two messages to be stored and played back with the push of a button - or text-to-speech programmes that will vocalise predictive text or typed words to generate novel information based on the user's desires. Voice and message banking are services offered to those who know they will lose their voices, but have enough vocal ability left to store that voice. Message banking is simpler: the user records numerous 'messages' (words and phrases) they anticipate needing, from the sound of a laugh, to calling a dog, to 'I love you' to daily requirements like food and hygiene. An extension of message banking is legacy banking, in which the user stores a particular story or message intended for a particular person - for example, a message to play her daughter on her wedding day. This is the service Bara offers. Voice banking is more sophisticated: the user records their own voice reading a set series of phrases that capture all the phonemes of the language. These are then used by a text-to-speech device to synthesis an electronic version of the user's own voice that sounds more or less like them. So far, this is not widely available in South Africa, and there are no local companies offering it. VocaliD is therefore a step above the rest, offering people who have never been able to speak the chance to have a synthesised voice that is unique to them, and contains something of their own vocalisation. Other companies exist that will create unique voices that are age-appropriate and might be generated from a donor's voice (a sibling for example). We will speak to Rupal Patel via Skype, and then bring the story home with various case studies and experts in South Africa. VocaliD does not have any South African users but they do have about 5 'voice bankers' so we will speak to one of them. We will visit the Bara clinic to watch a message banking session, interview a therapist and watch the clinic at work. We will then visit one of the MND/message banking patients at home to see how they use their recorded voice. We will interview a scientist at CSIR regarding the development of indigenous language AAC software. We will then visit New Hope School to speak to Alexander, a Grade 1 learner who makes use of the Afrikaans text-to-speech programme. We will speak to Kevin Jordan, an MND sufferer who uses eye gaze technology to communicate and to control the appliances in his house. Time permitting, we will interview someone from Inclusive Solutions, the company that imports the majority of AAC devices into South Africa. Desirae can demonstrate to us how the devices work, allow our presenter to try them out, and talk about some of the challenges that families face when they start using AAC.
